transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my family actually pushed me to make this appointment. They think I'm not handling things well since my dad passed, or that I'm too stressed. Which is ironic, because stress is pretty much my baseline right now anyway. I'm a systems analyst, and we're right in the middle of this massive server migration at work. It's been exhausting. I'm constantly staring at error logs and packet drops, trying to figure out where the discrepancies are. It actually reminds me a lot of when I was getting my degree and my database professor used to drill into us that the raw data always tells the real story, no matter what the front-end user interface tries to show you. 

And honestly, that's exactly what's happening here. That's all I'm doing. I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly. But... I look at data for a living. When I actually compare the timestamps, notice the missing attachments, and see the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions when I bring it up? It’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. But my family thinks I'm the one who needs to talk to someone, so here I am.

Before your father passed away, would you say you generally had this same level of suspicion about people hiding things from you, or is this a new way of thinking that started around the time of his death?

No, no, I wouldn't say I was like this before. I mean, sure, in my line of work you have to be detail-oriented, you have to look for the bugs, right? But with people? No. This... this all really started about nine months ago. Right after he died. That's when I started going through his records, you know, his emails, the hospital bills, trying to get his estate in order. 

It’s funny, actually, going through his stuff... I found this old pocket watch of his. I hadn’t seen it since I was a kid. He used to let me wind it up on Sunday mornings before church. We went to this little Methodist church on 4th Street—well, it was Methodist back then, I think it’s a community center now or something. They repainted the doors this awful shade of yellow. I don't know who picked that color, it completely clashes with the brickwork. Bricks need a cooler tone, like a slate blue or a forest green, otherwise it just looks cheap. But anyway, yeah, it’s been about nine months since I started noticing the discrepancies in his files.
Since your father passed, aside from these suspicions about the records, have you been feeling persistently sad, tearful, or overwhelmed with grief when you think about him?

Not really, no. I mean, I miss him, sure, but I haven't been sitting around crying or feeling overwhelmed by sadness. I've been too focused on figuring out the actual facts of what happened. Which, honestly, keeping busy helps. 

Like, I was looking at his old car the other day—he had this 1998 Honda Accord. He kept it in pristine condition. You know, they really don't manufacture vehicles like that anymore. Everything now is just packed with electronic bloat. My co-worker Dave bought a new SUV a few months ago, and the main console literally crashed on him while he was merging onto the highway. Can you imagine? Having to reboot your car's dashboard at 70 miles an hour? It just proves how terrible the QA testing is on consumer tech these days. They push these firmware updates over the air without even checking for memory leaks, just assuming the end-user will deal with the bugs. It’s completely irresponsible. If I pushed code like that at work, I'd be fired by lunch. 

But, um... sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the grief. Yeah, no, I haven't been tearful or depressed or anything like that.
Have you ever heard voices, seen things, or had any other unusual sensory experiences that other people don't seem to notice?

No, I haven't experienced anything like that. No voices or visions or anything. My brain works just fine, better than most people's, honestly. I rely on hard evidence, not imagination. 

Speaking of imagination, though, my niece—she's six—she has this imaginary friend named Bartholomew. It's fascinating how children's brains develop, isn't it? They just invent these entire personas out of thin air. She insists he sits at the dinner table with them. My sister actually sets a plate for him, which I think is just reinforcing the behavior, but she read some parenting blog that said you're supposed to validate their creative milestones. Those blogs are completely unregulated, by the way. Anyone can just buy a domain name and start giving psychological advice. I actually looked into the hosting data for one of the sites she sent me, and it was registered to some shell company in Cyprus. Makes you wonder what they're actually doing with the user data when you sign up for their newsletters. Probably selling it to ad networks or using it to train language models without consent. It's a massive privacy violation waiting to happen. 

But yeah, to answer your question, no, I don't hear or see things that aren't there. I'm strictly dealing with the facts in front of me.
Has this focus on your father's records affected your ability to concentrate at work, maintain relationships, or handle your daily responsibilities in any other way?

I mean, no, not really. I still go to work every day, I handle all my projects, pay my bills on time, you know, keep up with my normal routine. I actually just finished a massive server migration at work last week. We had to move everything from our legacy on-prem hardware to a hybrid cloud setup. The downtime was scheduled for 2:00 AM on Sunday, which is just the worst time because if something goes wrong, you're debugging at 4:00 AM on zero sleep. And of course, the vendor promised a seamless transition, but their API documentation was completely outdated. I had to manually rewrite half the scripts just to get the data to parse correctly. It's incredible how these massive enterprise companies can charge millions of dollars for software and then completely neglect their documentation. It's like buying a house and the builder gives you a map of a different neighborhood. I ended up writing a scathing email to their support team, but they just sent back an automated response. Typical. 

But anyway, yeah, work is fine. My daily stuff is fine. I guess the only place things get a little tense is... well, with my family or people around the community. Whenever I bring up the questions I have about my father's records, they get all defensive or try to change the subject. It's like nobody wants to look at the actual data.
